gates.title: Per-image licensing, archive capture, and public availability
gates.findings: Creator and publisher: Karen Kenworthy (karenware.com). Period and current page footers say All Rights Reserved. The only license on the site covers program use (free for personal and educational use), not reuse of website images. According to the site, Karen's intellectual property passed to family member Terry Starr, and Joe Winett operates the site. Access was an anonymous Wayback raw replay: no account, payment, terms, watermark, or CAPTCHA. Credit text is proposed only.
gates.reason: No permission or license on record for reuse of the screenshot. Public and archival availability is not permission.
gates.review_question: Should Devin ask the karenware.com operator for permission to show this screenshot, make a recorded fair-use decision, or leave it out of the collage? Sending the request is a human boundary.

gates.title: Popularity, installed base, prices, and real VB applications
gates.agent_check: passed for this image's VB provenance; narration claims out of scope
gates.findings: Implementation language is documented independently of the image's appearance. (1) The author's September 28, 1999 newsletter offers the program's Visual Basic 6.0 source code. (2) The 2001 and 2003 download pages require the Visual Basic Runtime v6.0 and offer VB6 source code. (3) The screenshot itself shows the program's own button reporting module MSVBVM60.DLL and class ThunderRT6CommandButton. The asset makes no statistic, ranking, price, or popularity claim, and adds no caption. It does not evidence the narration's broad claims in SCRIPT.md:685 (accountants, teachers, small business owners, non-programmers); those stay routed to the producer.
limitations: The image is a 2003 capture on a Windows XP-style desktop of a VB6 utility first introduced in 1999, not a mid-1990s VB3/VB4 program.
The author was a Windows Magazine columnist who published utilities for readers, so the example does not show a self-described non-programmer.
gates.reason: Agent evidence recorded; the review deck decides release and narration fit.
gates.review_question: The image is a 2003 Windows XP capture of a 1999 VB6 utility by a magazine columnist. Is that acceptable as the collage's 'simple utility' beside narration set in VB's early years about non-programmers, or should the collage keep looking for a VB3/VB4-era example?
